keyVerseText: And he set a carved image, the idol which he had made, in the house of God, of which God had said to David and to Solomon his son, In this house, and in Jerusalem, which I have chosen before all the tribes of Israel, will I put my name for ever:
rootMeaning: The Hebrew noun עֵילוֹם (ʻêylôwm) is etymologically connected to the root word עוֹלָם (ʻôwlâm), which conveys the idea of something concealed or hidden, like a vanishing point beyond human perception. This root emphasizes a sense of endless duration or perpetuity, extending beyond measurable time into the realm of the eternal. Thus, while the English gloss 'forever' captures the temporal aspect, the root meaning deepens the understanding to include the concept of an unfathomable, concealed permanence that transcends human history.
usageInScripture: This word appears only once in Scripture, translated as 'for ever' in 2 Chronicles 33:7. Its singular occurrence underscores a consistent meaning focused on perpetuity or everlasting duration. The translation 'for ever' reflects the word's role in expressing a divine promise or condition that endures beyond temporal limits, highlighting the unchanging and eternal nature of God's presence and covenant.
theologicalSignificance: Understanding עֵילוֹם as rooted in the concept of concealed, eternal duration enriches Christian faith by framing God's promises and presence as not merely long-lasting but transcendent and unfathomable. It reminds believers that God's covenantal faithfulness is anchored in an eternal, unchanging reality beyond human comprehension. This eternal aspect assures Christians of God's perpetual commitment and the everlasting nature of His kingdom, reinforcing hope grounded in divine constancy rather than temporal circumstances.
keyVerseReflection: In 2 Chronicles 33:7, the phrase 'will I put my name for ever' uses עֵילוֹם to affirm God's enduring presence in the temple and Jerusalem. This word conveys that God's choice and the indwelling of His name are not temporary but eternally fixed, reflecting His unbreakable covenant with Israel. The use of עֵילוֹם here emphasizes the perpetual sanctity of the place God has chosen, assuring that His divine authority and relationship with His people are everlasting.
